newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Non-ferrous metals demand outlook bright - BBL.
newsitem.headline: Non-ferrous metals demand outlook bright - BBL.

text.p: Demand for non-ferrous metals such as zinc and copper in future looks bright due to expanding new technologies, but the price outlook is rather more mixed, Belgium's Banque Bruxelles Lambert said on Wednesday.
"Non-ferrous metals are promised a bright future," BBL said in monthly economic report dedicated in April to non-ferrous metals.

"Cadmium and indium are intensively used in electricity and electronics, while lead still benefits from the rising sales of car batteries. As for copper...it remains irreplaceable for carrying electricity," the bank added.
Zinc, the third most important non-ferrous metal after aluminium and copper, also has a strong future -- although it is not as geared towards new technologies as the others, BBL said.
"We think that the price of zinc will at least remain at the current level.

"The approach of the critical threshold (between supply and demand) might even cause some panic regardless of the fact that the general climate seems less prone to the exaggerations of the past," BBL said.
"We estimate an average price of $1,300 a tonnes during 1997 and of $1,400 in 1998," the bank said.
For copper, however, BBL predicted that prices would fall as supply grew four percent a year to the end of the century, but demand only grew by two percent a year.
"As a result the market price for copper will tend to decline. $2,150 a tonne in 1997 and $2,000 in 1998 according to us," it said.
Further ahead, the picture might improve as demand rose strongly from the emerging economies, although much would depend on the degree of substitution by other materials, the bank noted.
Lead prices are also seen falling, with BBL predicting an average of $740 a tonne this year, declining to $700 a tonne in 1998 due to high volumes coming into Europe from the east and China.
However, the bank remained overall optimistic for the whole non-ferrous metals sector while remaining mindful of the challenges posed by substitution and the timing of the business cycle.
